citation.author: Iain Donald and Andrew Reid
citation.title: The Wild West: Accuracy, Authenticity and Gameplay in Red Dead Redemption 2

thesis: Historical accuracy (alignment with the established record) and historical authenticity (subjective feeling rooted in collective memory) are distinct concepts; RDR2 is not historically accurate but feels authentic because Rockstar weaves fact and fiction so expertly that players forgive discrepancies. The deeper aim is pedagogical: read games as 'historical text' via the tripartite frame account/accuracy/authenticity to use RDR2 in the history classroom.
sections: Framing (sandbox genre; Red Dead series continuity 1880s/1899/1911)
Account (Fullerton formal vs. dramatic elements; Fernandez-Vara game analysis as content analysis)
Accuracy (material accuracy; characters exempt from record; modern-day lens)
Characters: Van der Linde Gang; Pinkerton Detective Agency; Murfree Brood
Environment: Declining Wild West; Encampments; Saint Denis

Next Steps (concepts 'nebulous'; game as teaching gateway not history lesson)
concepts: accuracy (alignment with established historical record: timeline + material detail)
authenticity (subjective feeling of period rooted in communal/collective memory)
material accuracy (organisations, events, buildings, outfits, objects)
formal elements vs. dramatic elements (Fullerton: game 'layers')
game analysis as content analysis (Fernandez-Vara: games as text)
weaving fact and fiction (gaps in the historical record)
modern lens on the past (thought, action, journalism 'modernised')
readings: The Western genre is film-mediated: RDR2's authenticity is cinematic before it is historical (Murfree Brood indebted to Deliverance/The Hills Have Eyes/Ravenous/Bone Tomahawk).
Characters are composites/caricatures, not portraits: Dutch Van der Linde from Butch Cassidy 'mythos' as framework, not account; Leviticus Cornwall amalgamates Vanderbilt/J.P. Morgan/Carnegie.
Environment is fictional place rooted in real time: Saint Denis as fictionalised New Orleans (Plessy v. Ferguson segregation echo; St. Denis of Paris allusion).
In-game newspapers are an authenticity-effect, not a record: jingoistic 'yellow journalism' tone, simplified and modernised.
Authenticity, not accuracy, binds the player: the game does not teach history but invites players to 'play with history.'
Rockstar evokes industry/labour/colonialism but 'stop short' of social commentary (anti-imperialism absent) — authentic feeling without critique.

game_elements.how_treated: Read as authentic-feeling fictionalisation of New Orleans: Jackson Square -> 'Harris Square'; David Hennessy murder -> in-game Henry Jenkins murder + New Orleans lynchings; optional saloon vermin-control mission; Nosferatu/Count Orlok vampire side-encounter; segregated design echoing Plessy v. Ferguson.

Gilded-Age-to-progressivism transition as template of conflicting beliefs; environmental change (new properties, deforestation, completed railway) signals ideological change; painting sources (Bierstadt 'Among the Sierra Nevada'; N. C. Wyeth 'Hands Up!') for lighting/composition.

Strategic camp system (near towns=supplies; near rivers=food/water; fortresses=defence); Horseshoe Overlook reflects Wyoming's Hole-in-the-Wall Pass (Wild Bunch); transitory camp movement 'projects the feeling of insecurity, paranoia.'
Composited from Dalton Gang, Doolin-Dalton Gang, and Butch Cassidy's Wild Bunch; Dutch from Cassidy mythos as 'framework rather than an accurate account'; player as Arthur Morgan, enforcer.

Real agency (founded by Scotsman Allan Pinkerton, 1850; anti-labour/strikebreaking history); use prompted a real cease-and-desist; Take-Two counter-filed on fair use ('game emphasises historical authenticity'), settled out of court — authenticity with real-world legal stakes ('Who Owns History?').

Cannibal-clan; arguably inspired by Levi Boone Helm and the Sawney Bean legend, but read as 'more obvious[ly]' film-based (Deliverance, The Hills Have Eyes, Ravenous, Bone Tomahawk) — authenticity via cinematic trope.

game_elements.element: Union Pacific Overland Flyer Robbery ('Who the Hell is Leviticus Cornwall?', mission 5)
game_elements.how_treated: Plays the Western train-robbery trope; modelled on the 1899 Wilcox Robbery by the Wild Bunch (timeline tie-in 'largely fortuitous'); in-game leaping-aboard diverges from real flag-down + dynamite-on-mail-cars; introduces Cornwall as 'parodic caricature' of robber barons.
game_elements.locus: Events > Union Pacific Overland Flyer Robbery

game_elements.how_treated: Fictional President Alfred MacAlister ~ McKinley; Col. Thaddeus Waxman ~ Theodore Roosevelt Jr.; Battle of San Juan Hill relocated to fictional 'Guarma' (fictitious Cuba); Treaty of Paris + Philippine Insurrection referenced; newspapers as chief authenticity-vector, jingoistic 'yellow journalism' but simplified/modernised.
Composited from Liddell-Jones and Hatfield-McCoy feuds; player situated as 'external force' whose intervention drives a dramatised, blood-soaked resolution that 'veers wildly from the accounts.'
game_elements.locus: Events > Civic Unrest in the Reconstruction Era

game_elements.how_treated: Subsumed under 'material accuracy' — 'the factual use of organisations, events, buildings, outfits and objects' — as the believability-anchoring layer that enables immersion, not analysed as a standalone case.

debate_axis_positions.position: Strongly authenticity-as-feel; the article explicitly NAMES the axis and separates accuracy (record-alignment) from authenticity (subjective feeling rooted in collective memory).
debate_axis_positions.evidence: 'authenticity is about creating a feeling for the gameplay experience that feels correct in order to be immersed'; RDR2 'not historically accurate' yet authentic; accuracy treated as instrumental to feel (material accuracy serves believability -> immersion).

debate_axis_positions.axis: accuracy as measure vs. accuracy as servant
debate_axis_positions.position: Accuracy is the servant of authenticity, not its measure; material accuracy exists to make immersion possible.
debate_axis_positions.evidence: 'The accuracy of the material detail is fundamental to constructing a gameworld that is believable.'

debate_axis_positions.axis: game as history-teacher vs. game as inquiry-gateway
debate_axis_positions.position: Inquiry-gateway: RDR2 'is not a game that teaches history' but opens 'new ways of exploring' American Expansionism.
debate_axis_positions.evidence: Next Steps; 'play with history to understand the world of the protagonist.'

tensions: Authors concede all three concepts are 'at best nebulous,' undercutting the frame's promised rigour.
Accuracy is named as distinct but repeatedly subordinated to authenticity, leaving it little independent evaluative force.
Authenticity grounded in collective memory, yet worked examples trace that memory to FILM, risking circularity (feels authentic = matches our movies).
Depoliticisation (Rockstar evokes colonialism/labour 'without complexity') is noted approvingly rather than problematised.
Pedagogical aim (history classroom) sits in tension with the admission that the game does not teach history; payoff rests on critical comparison, not game content.
